fixes.explanation: That's it, baker. Isaiah's message opens with “Because you have prayed to Me concerning Sennacherib king of Assyria…” so the LORD is answering Hezekiah's prayer. Sennacherib was Assyria's king, the one Hezekiah prayed about. I think prayer is a pretty good thing to do when somebody that big is on your mind.

This one's true, friend. In his bragging Sennacherib, Assyria's king, says, “I have cut down its tallest cedars, the finest of its cypresses.” The LORD quotes his own words back to him. I bet that man had a LOT to say about those trees.

Yes, baker, false. The LORD says the people are “…like plants in the field, tender green shoots, grass on the rooftops, scorched before it is grown.” That's a picture of weakness, nothing like a mighty tree. Grass on a rooftop, scorched before it is grown. Not much of a tree.

Not at all, friend. The LORD says, “But I know your sitting down, your going out and coming in, and your raging against Me.” He says that about Sennacherib, Assyria's king. His raging was known to the LORD.

Right, baker, false. The LORD says to Sennacherib, Assyria's king, “But I know your sitting down, your going out and coming in, and your raging against Me.” The raging is right there on the LORD's list.

You got it, baker. The LORD says, “I will send you back the way you came.” Sennacherib, Assyria's king, is the one getting the hook in his nose and the bit in his mouth. I think that's a man being steered.

That's a different king, friend. The LORD asks, “Whom have you taunted and blasphemed?” and the answer in the text is “Against the Holy One of Israel!” Sennacherib was Assyria's king, and the verse never brings up Babylon. That's a much bigger target than any king.

The LORD says the opposite, friend. He says Sennacherib, Assyria's king, “…will not enter this city or shoot an arrow into it. He will not come before it with a shield or build up a siege ramp against it.” The LORD says he will not build one against it.

Yes, baker. The LORD says, “I will defend this city and save it for My own sake and for the sake of My servant David.” He's the One doing the defending, and He names Himself first. I think that's a good promise to hear.

Yes, baker, Ararat. The text says Adrammelech and Sharezer, Sennacherib's sons, “…escaped to the land of Ararat.” This is a heavy part of the passage, so I'll just say it plainly. Ararat is the land the text names.
That name isn't in this passage, baker. The text says, “And his son Esar-haddon reigned in his place.” It's Sennacherib's own son who takes the throne. Esar-haddon is the name the verse gives.
